items.prompt: How do I make sure that even a production administrator cannot turn off the audit log?
items.ten_second: Use an organization trail from the management account. Member accounts, their administrators included, can see the trail but can't change or delete it.
sixty_second: The short answer is: make the audit log an organization trail in the management account.
It works like this. One organization trail logs every account.
Member accounts can see that trail, but they can't change it or delete it.
That includes the production administrator, because production is a member account.
Keep the log files in a separate log archive account, protected from changes.
For other rules, add a service control policy that denies the action.
Even an administrator with full access can't use an action that the SCP blocks.
The thing to watch is the management account itself.
SCPs don't limit the users or roles in that account.
Keep workloads out of it, and give very few people access.
In your case, production stays a member account, so its administrators can't change the trail.
Who can sign in to the management account today?

key_points.point: An organization trail logs events for all accounts, and member accounts can see it but cannot modify or delete it.
accept: production can see the trail but can't turn it off
member accounts can't change the organization trail

key_points.point: You create an organization trail from the management account or a delegated administrator account.
accept: the trail is created in the management account
a delegated administrator can create it too

key_points.point: If an SCP above the account blocks a permission, users and roles in that account cannot use it, even with AdministratorAccess.
accept: an SCP deny holds against the administrator
full admin rights can't override the SCP

key_points.point: SCPs do not restrict users or roles in the management account, so AWS recommends keeping resources out of it.
accept: the management account is outside the SCPs
keep workloads out of the management account

key_points.point: The log archive account consolidates log data from all accounts, and its log data is protected from being changed or deleted.
accept: a separate account for the logs
the log archive account keeps the logs safe

key_points.point: Control Tower preventive controls are not applied to the management account, but its actions are still logged.
accept: Control Tower controls skip the management account

must_not_say.error: an SCP on the root also stops the management account from changing the trail
must_not_say.correct: SCPs affect only member accounts. They do not restrict users or roles in the management account.

must_not_say.error: the production account can't even see the organization trail
must_not_say.correct: Member accounts can see the organization trail, but they cannot modify or delete it.

must_not_say.error: an administrator with AdministratorAccess in production can turn the SCP off for that account
must_not_say.correct: If an SCP above the account blocks a permission, users and roles in that account cannot use it, even with AdministratorAccess.

follow_ups.question: What if someone deletes the log bucket instead of the trail?
follow_ups.answer: In a Control Tower landing zone, mandatory controls on the Security OU prevent deletion of the S3 buckets that Control Tower creates in the log archive account. From Landing Zone version 4.0, check that they are applied: they are no longer applied by default.

follow_ups.question: Can the people in the management account change the trail?
follow_ups.answer: SCPs do not restrict them, and Control Tower preventive controls are not applied to the management account. Their actions are still logged, so keep very few people there.

items.prompt: Do we need AWS Control Tower, or is AWS Organizations enough?
items.ten_second: Both manage many accounts. Organizations is the framework. Control Tower builds and governs the accounts on top of it, with ready-made controls.
sixty_second: Both help you run many AWS accounts from one place.
The difference is that Control Tower builds and governs the accounts for you.
It works like this. Organizations is the framework: accounts, organizational units, policies and one bill.
Control Tower is the automation and governance layer on top of it.
It builds a landing zone, a well-architected environment of many accounts.
Account Factory creates each new account from a template, with controls applied.
The thing to watch is cost. Control Tower has no charge of its own.
But you pay for the services it turns on, like AWS Config.
Short-lived resources, like Spot workers, can raise the AWS Config bill.
In your case, size decides. AWS suggests Control Tower for more than a handful of accounts.
How many accounts will you have next year, and who will create them?

key_points.point: AWS describes Organizations as the framework and Control Tower as the automation and governance layer on top of it.
accept: Control Tower sits on top of Organizations
Organizations is the base, Control Tower automates it

key_points.point: Control Tower extends the capabilities of AWS Organizations and applies controls to keep accounts from drifting away from best practices.
accept: Control Tower adds controls to Organizations
it keeps accounts from drifting

key_points.point: Account Factory is a configurable account template that automates applying controls and policies to new accounts.
accept: new accounts come from a template
Account Factory applies the controls for you

key_points.point: Control Tower has no additional charge, but you pay for the services it enables, such as AWS Config and CloudTrail.
accept: free itself, but you pay for AWS Config
you pay for the underlying services

key_points.point: AWS says that with more than a handful of accounts, an orchestration layer such as Control Tower helps with account deployment and governance.
accept: Control Tower pays off with more than a few accounts

key_points.point: Ephemeral workloads in Control Tower accounts can increase AWS Config costs, because AWS Config records each create and delete.
accept: short-lived resources raise the AWS Config bill

key_points.point: AWS Organizations is offered at no additional charge.
accept: Organizations itself is free

must_not_say.error: Control Tower replaces Organizations, so you pick one of the two
must_not_say.correct: Control Tower extends the capabilities of AWS Organizations. It works on top of Organizations, not instead of it.

must_not_say.error: Control Tower costs nothing to run
must_not_say.correct: Control Tower has no additional charge, but you pay for the services it enables, such as AWS Config and CloudTrail.

follow_ups.question: Can we add Control Tower later, to the organization we already have?
follow_ups.answer: Yes. You register the existing OUs and enroll the existing accounts. Until you do, accounts and OUs created outside Control Tower are not bound by its controls.

follow_ups.question: Do the Control Tower controls stop a bad action, or only report it?
follow_ups.answer: It depends on the type. Preventive controls prevent actions from occurring. Detective controls detect events when they occur and alert through the dashboard. Proactive controls check resources before they are provisioned.
